summary: This chapter covers how the human body works and stays healthy: body systems, homeostasis, nutrition, and disease. The GED Science test uses these ideas in its Human Health and Living Systems theme, often with a short passage, a food label, or a data table.

Body systems work together. Muscles pull on bones to move the body, and the nervous and endocrine systems send signals that control other organs. Homeostasis is the body's way of keeping inside conditions steady. Most of it works by negative feedback: the body senses a change and responds in the opposite direction, such as sweating when hot or releasing insulin when blood sugar rises.

Food gives the body energy and building materials. Carbohydrates are the main quick energy source, and fat stores the most energy per gram. Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts but contain no calories. Diseases are caused by pathogens (germs) that spread through the air, water, food, blood, or contact. They are prevented by methods such as vaccination, hand washing, sanitation, and protective equipment.

concepts.definition: Keeping inside conditions such as body temperature, blood sugar, and water balance steady, even when the outside changes.
concepts.tip: Sweating when hot and shivering when cold are classic examples.

concepts.definition: A response that reverses a change. Blood sugar rises, insulin is released, and blood sugar falls back.
concepts.tip: Negative feedback = bring it back to normal.

concepts.definition: Groups of organs that do a job. Muscular and skeletal systems move the body; the circulatory system carries blood; the endocrine system makes hormones.
concepts.tip: Ask which systems must work together for the job described.

concepts.definition: Fat has about 9 Calories per gram; carbohydrate and protein have about 4 each. Vitamins, minerals, and water have none.
concepts.tip: Multiply grams by Calories per gram for each nutrient, then add.

concepts.definition: A germ that causes disease, such as a virus or bacterium. It can spread through air, water, food, blood, or contact.
concepts.tip: Match the precaution to the way the germ spreads.

concepts.definition: Trains the immune system to recognize a germ before a person is exposed, so the body can fight it off quickly.
concepts.tip: Vaccines prevent; antibiotics treat bacterial infections.

points: Sweating cools the body by evaporation; narrowing skin blood vessels saves heat in the cold.
Insulin lowering blood sugar is negative feedback.
Gloves protect against bloodborne germs; covering coughs protects against airborne germs.
A supported conclusion describes what the data show; it does not claim proof from a small study.

compare.title: How diseases spread and how to block them
rows: Washing hands and food, cooking, clean water

summary: This chapter explains how living things get the energy they need. Plants capture energy from sunlight, and almost all living things release energy from food through cellular respiration.

In photosynthesis, plants and algae use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. It takes place in chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll. In cellular respiration, cells use oxygen to break down glucose, releasing energy and giving off carbon dioxide and water. It takes place in the mitochondria.

The two processes are linked: each uses what the other produces. When oxygen is short, some cells, including human muscle cells during hard exercise, use fermentation, which releases a small amount of energy without oxygen and makes lactic acid in muscle. GED questions on this topic often describe a simple experiment, such as counting oxygen bubbles from a water plant under a lamp.

concepts.definition: Carbon dioxide + water + light energy → glucose + oxygen. Happens in chloroplasts.
concepts.tip: Plants make food and give off oxygen.

concepts.definition: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy. Happens in mitochondria.
concepts.tip: Respiration is not the same as breathing; it happens inside cells.

concepts.definition: Releasing energy from glucose without oxygen. In human muscle it makes lactic acid; yeast makes alcohol and carbon dioxide.
concepts.tip: No oxygen, less energy.

concepts.definition: Chloroplasts capture light for photosynthesis. Mitochondria release energy from food.
concepts.tip: Chloroplast = capture light; mitochondrion = release energy.

concepts.definition: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy. One glucose makes 6 carbon dioxide molecules.
concepts.tip: Multiply by the number of glucose molecules used.

points: The products of photosynthesis are the reactants of respiration, and the reverse.
In a lamp-distance experiment, distance (light) is the independent variable and bubbles counted is the dependent variable.
Describe the trend in data without claiming an exact pattern the numbers do not show.

summary: This chapter covers how energy and matter move through ecosystems and how populations affect one another. GED questions often show a food web or energy pyramid and ask what happens when one population changes.

Producers such as plants make their own food from sunlight. Consumers eat other organisms, and decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil. In a food chain or food web, arrows point from the food to the organism that eats it, showing the direction energy flows. Only about 10% of the energy at one level passes to the next; the rest is used for life processes or lost as heat. That is why an energy pyramid gets narrower at the top.

Populations are limited by food, water, space, and predators. The largest population an area can support over time is its carrying capacity. Organisms also interact through symbiosis: in mutualism both benefit, in commensalism one benefits and the other is not affected, and in parasitism one benefits and the host is harmed. Invasive species, habitat destruction, and other disruptions can upset these relationships and cause local extinctions.

concepts.definition: Producers make food from sunlight. Consumers eat other organisms. Decomposers break down dead matter and recycle nutrients.
concepts.tip: Producers have no arrows coming in from food.

concepts.definition: Each arrow points from the food to the eater, showing the direction energy flows.
concepts.tip: Follow the arrow: grass → rabbit means the rabbit eats grass.

concepts.definition: About 10% of the energy at one level passes to the next level. Example: 10,000 kcal in producers → 1,000 → 100 → 10.
concepts.tip: Multiply by 0.1 for each step up.

concepts.definition: The largest population an environment can support over time. A population that levels off is near its carrying capacity.
concepts.tip: Look for where the population levels off.

concepts.definition: Mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, other unaffected), parasitism (one benefits, host harmed).
concepts.tip: Ask who benefits and who is harmed.

concepts.definition: A non-native species that spreads in a new area and harms the ecosystem, often because it has no natural predators there.
concepts.tip: Native = always lived there; invasive = brought in and spreading.

points: If an animal has only one food source, it is hit hardest when that food declines.
Fewer predators usually means more prey, at least for a while.
Mark-recapture estimate: tagged in sample ÷ sample size = total tagged ÷ total population.
Habitat destruction usually lowers the number of species in an area.

figures.alt: Energy pyramid with four levels. Producers at the bottom have 10,000 kcal, primary consumers 1,000 kcal, secondary consumers 100 kcal, and tertiary consumers at the top 10 kcal.
figures.caption: About 10% of the energy passes up to each next level, so the pyramid narrows toward the top.

summary: This chapter covers cells, the basic units of life, and how they are organized into larger structures. It also explains how cells divide.

The cell theory says that all living things are made of cells, the cell is the smallest unit of life, and new cells come only from existing cells. Inside a cell, the cell membrane controls what enters and leaves, the nucleus holds the DNA, ribosomes make proteins, and mitochondria release energy. Plant cells also have a cell wall and chloroplasts. Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions; they work best at a certain temperature, and too much heat changes their shape so they stop working well.

In many-celled organisms, similar cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs work together in organ systems. Cells divide by mitosis to grow and repair: one cell makes two identical cells. Meiosis makes sex cells (eggs and sperm) with half the usual number of chromosomes, 23 in humans instead of 46.

concepts.definition: All living things are made of cells; the cell is the smallest unit of life; cells come from existing cells.
concepts.tip: Cells come only from cells.

concepts.definition: The outer boundary of the cell. It controls what moves in and out.
concepts.tip: Think of it as the cell's gatekeeper.

concepts.definition: Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.
concepts.tip: Each level is made of the one before it.

concepts.definition: A protein that speeds up a chemical reaction. It has a best (optimum) temperature; high heat changes its shape and slows it.
concepts.tip: Activity rises to a peak, then falls if it gets too hot.

concepts.definition: Cell division that makes two identical cells with the full number of chromosomes. Used for growth and repair.
concepts.tip: Mitosis = make more of the same.

concepts.definition: Cell division that makes sex cells with half the number of chromosomes. Human body cells have 46; eggs and sperm have 23.
concepts.tip: Meiosis = half the chromosomes, for sex cells.

points: Signs of life include taking in nutrients, using energy, and reproducing.
The best temperature for an enzyme is the highest point in the activity data.
Mitosis: 2 identical cells. Meiosis: 4 sex cells with half the chromosomes.

summary: This chapter explains how traits are passed from parents to children. GED questions often ask you to complete a Punnett square, read a pedigree chart, or explain how genes and the environment work together.

DNA in chromosomes carries genes, the instructions for traits. Genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to protein, which is called the central dogma. Each person has two alleles (versions) of most genes, one from each parent. A dominant allele shows its trait even with one copy; a recessive trait shows only when both alleles are recessive. The genotype is the pair of alleles, such as Pp, and the phenotype is the trait you can see, such as purple flowers.

A Punnett square shows the possible offspring of two parents. A cross of two carriers (Pp × Pp) gives 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp, so there is a 25% chance of the recessive trait. Mutations are changes in DNA that can create new alleles, and meiosis mixes alleles so that brothers and sisters differ. The environment can also affect how a gene is expressed; for example, the dark fur on a Siamese cat's cooler body parts depends on temperature.

concepts.definition: One version of a gene. A person usually has two alleles for each gene, one from each parent.
concepts.tip: One from mom, one from dad.

concepts.definition: A dominant allele (capital letter) shows with one copy. A recessive allele (small letter) shows only when there are two copies.
concepts.tip: Pp shows the dominant trait; only pp shows the recessive one.

concepts.definition: Genotype is the allele pair (such as Pp). Phenotype is the observable trait (such as purple flowers).
concepts.tip: Genotype = letters; phenotype = what you see.

concepts.definition: A grid that shows possible offspring. Pp × Pp → 25% PP, 50% Pp, 25% pp. Pp × pp → 50% Pp, 50% pp.
concepts.tip: Each box is 25%.

concepts.definition: DNA → RNA → protein. DNA is copied into RNA, and RNA is read to build a protein.
concepts.tip: DNA → RNA → protein, in that order.

concepts.definition: A change in the DNA base sequence. Mutations are the source of new alleles.
concepts.tip: Mutations can be harmful, helpful, or have no effect.

points: Two parents without a trait who have a child with it: the trait is recessive and both parents are carriers.
Check whether the question asks for the dominant or recessive trait before choosing a percent.
The environment can change how a gene is expressed without changing the DNA.

summary: This chapter covers how populations change over many generations and the evidence that living things share common ancestors. GED questions often describe a population over time or show a cladogram.

Natural selection needs inherited variation: individuals differ in traits that can be passed on. When some traits help individuals survive and reproduce in their environment, those traits become more common over generations. Examples include bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics and dark peppered moths becoming more common on soot-darkened trees. When people choose which plants or animals breed, it is artificial selection.

Evidence of common ancestry includes similar bone structures in different species, such as the front limbs of humans, whales, and bats. A cladogram is a branching diagram of relationships; groups that share a more recent branch point are more closely related. When a population is split by a barrier, the groups can change until they can no longer interbreed, forming new species. This is speciation.

concepts.definition: Individuals with helpful inherited traits survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common over generations.
concepts.tip: Populations change, not individuals.

concepts.definition: People choose which organisms breed to get desired traits, such as cows that give more milk.
concepts.tip: People choose = artificial; the environment chooses = natural.

concepts.definition: An inherited trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.
concepts.tip: Adaptations are inherited, not learned during one lifetime.

concepts.definition: Body parts with the same basic bones but different jobs, such as human arms and bat wings. They suggest common ancestry.
concepts.tip: Same bones, different jobs.

concepts.definition: A branching diagram. A more recent shared branch point means a closer relationship.
concepts.tip: Read from the branch points, not from left to right.

concepts.definition: Formation of a new species, often after groups are separated and can no longer interbreed.
concepts.tip: A barrier plus many generations can make new species.

points: Organisms do not change their traits on purpose; selection acts on variation that already exists.
Antibiotic resistance is natural selection in action.
A cladogram does not show one living species turning into another.

summary: This chapter covers energy: its forms, how it changes from one form to another, how heat moves, and how waves carry energy. It is part of the Energy and Related Systems theme on the GED Science test.

Energy is not created or destroyed; it changes form. A raised object has gravitational potential energy, and a moving object has kinetic energy. A battery stores chemical energy that becomes electrical energy and then light and heat in a flashlight. Efficiency is the share of energy that becomes the useful form. Energy sources can be renewable, like sunlight and wind, or nonrenewable, like coal, oil, and natural gas.

Heat flows from hot to cold by conduction (direct contact), convection (moving liquid or gas), and radiation (waves that can cross empty space). Temperature is not the same as heat: more matter needs more heat for the same temperature change. Exothermic reactions release heat, and endothermic reactions absorb it.

Waves are described by frequency and wavelength, and wave speed = frequency × wavelength. The electromagnetic spectrum runs from radio waves (lowest frequency) through visible light to X-rays and gamma rays (highest). Ultraviolet light causes sunburn. Sound is a mechanical wave that needs matter to travel.

concepts.definition: Energy changes form but the total stays the same. Falling: potential energy → kinetic energy.
concepts.tip: Lost potential energy = gained kinetic energy (no air resistance).

concepts.definition: Potential energy is stored (for example, PE = mass × g × height). Kinetic energy is energy of motion.
concepts.tip: High up = potential; moving = kinetic.

concepts.definition: Conduction: through contact. Convection: by moving fluid. Radiation: by electromagnetic waves, even through empty space.
concepts.tip: Touch, flow, or waves.

concepts.definition: Exothermic reactions release heat (hand warmers). Endothermic reactions absorb heat (cold packs).
concepts.tip: Exo = exit (heat goes out); endo = enter (heat goes in).

concepts.definition: Speed = frequency × wavelength.
Low to high frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray.
concepts.tip: Higher frequency means more energy (UV, X-rays, gamma).

concepts.definition: Useful energy out ÷ energy in × 100. The rest usually becomes heat.
concepts.tip: Divide the useful part by the total, then multiply by 100.

points: A control group (such as an unwrapped can) shows what happens without the factor being tested.
The best insulator is the material with the smallest temperature drop.
Wind, sunlight, and moving water are renewable; coal, oil, and natural gas are not.
Sound cannot travel through empty space; light can.

compare.title: Three ways heat moves
rows: Through direct contact, mainly in solids
Hot soup warming a metal spoon
Warm air rising from a heater
By electromagnetic waves, even through space

summary: This chapter covers how things move and the forces that change their motion. On the GED test, a question gives you any formula it needs, so practice using a formula and reading motion from a table or graph.

Speed is distance divided by time, and acceleration is the change in speed divided by time. Momentum is mass times velocity, so a light object moving fast can have more momentum than a heavy object moving slowly. Newton's first law says objects keep their motion unless a force acts (inertia). The second law says force = mass × acceleration. The third law says every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

Mass is the amount of matter and stays the same everywhere; weight is the pull of gravity on that mass (weight = mass × g, with g about 9.8 m/s² on Earth). Without air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate. Friction acts against motion.

Work is force times distance, and power is work divided by time. Simple machines, such as levers, pulleys, ramps (inclined planes), wedges, screws, and wheels and axles, make work easier by trading force for distance. Mechanical advantage = output force ÷ input force.

concepts.definition: Speed = distance ÷ time. Acceleration = change in speed ÷ time.
concepts.tip: Write the formula first, then put in the numbers.

concepts.definition: 1st: inertia. 2nd: force = mass × acceleration. 3rd: equal and opposite reaction.
concepts.tip: First = keeps moving; second = F = ma; third = push back.

concepts.definition: Mass (kg) does not change from place to place. Weight (N) = mass × g and depends on gravity; g is about 9.8 m/s² on Earth.
concepts.tip: On Earth, weight = mass × 9.8 m/s². On the Moon, weight drops but mass stays.

concepts.definition: Momentum = mass × velocity.
concepts.tip: Multiply before you compare; the heaviest object may not win.

concepts.definition: Work = force × distance (joules). Power = work ÷ time (watts).
concepts.tip: Work multiplies; power divides by time.

concepts.definition: Lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, wedge, screw. Mechanical advantage = output force ÷ input force.
concepts.tip: Less force always means more distance.

points: On a distance-time table, distance that stays the same means the object is stopped.
Average speed for an interval uses only the distance and time for that interval.
A common mistake is dividing when the formula multiplies, or the reverse.

summary: This chapter covers what matter is made of, how it changes, and how chemical reactions are written. You do not need to memorize the periodic table, but you should recognize common element names and symbols.

Atoms contain protons (positive) and neutrons (no charge) in the nucleus, with electrons (negative) around it. A physical change, such as melting, boiling, or cutting, changes form but not the substance. A chemical change makes a new substance; signs include gas bubbles, a color change, heat or light, or a new solid.

Density is mass divided by volume. An object floats in a liquid if it is less dense than the liquid, and liquids that do not mix stack with the least dense on top. The volume of an odd-shaped solid can be found by how much it raises the water level.

A balanced chemical equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides, because mass is conserved: atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed. The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first and sets how much product can form. In a solution, the solvent dissolves the solute. Most solids dissolve better in hotter solvents, and a saturated solution holds all the solute it can at that temperature.

concepts.definition: Protons (+) and neutrons (no charge) in the nucleus; electrons (−) around the nucleus.
concepts.tip: Electron = negative; proton = positive.

concepts.definition: Physical: same substance, new form (melting, boiling). Chemical: new substance (rusting, burning).
concepts.tip: Ask: is it still the same substance?

concepts.definition: Density = mass ÷ volume. Less dense than water (1.0 g/cm³) floats.
concepts.tip: Less dense floats; more dense sinks.

concepts.definition: In a closed system, total mass before a reaction equals total mass after.
concepts.tip: Gas has mass too.

concepts.definition: Same number of each atom on both sides. Example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
concepts.tip: Change only the big numbers in front, never the small ones.

concepts.definition: The reactant that runs out first; it decides how much product forms.
concepts.tip: Use the equation's ratio to see which one runs out.

concepts.definition: Solvent dissolves; solute is dissolved. Saturated means no more solute can dissolve at that temperature.
concepts.tip: In salt water, water is the solvent and salt is the solute.

points: Common symbols: H hydrogen, O oxygen, C carbon, N nitrogen, Na sodium, Fe iron.
Volume of a rock = rise in water level in a measuring cylinder.
Gas made in a sealed bag still has mass, so the total mass does not change.
Being able to burn is a chemical property; melting point and shine are physical properties.

compare.title: Physical and chemical changes
rows: Change in shape, size, or state
Gas, color change, heat or light, new solid

summary: This chapter connects Earth's systems with living things: how matter cycles, where our energy and resources come from, and how people prepare for natural hazards. Questions often use a data table or a short description of a town's plan.

Matter moves in cycles. In the water cycle, water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation, and flows back to the ocean. In the carbon cycle, photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the air, while respiration, burning, and volcanoes add it. In the nitrogen cycle, soil bacteria change nitrogen gas into forms plants can use. Fossil fuels formed over millions of years from buried ancient plants and sea organisms, so they are nonrenewable.

Renewable resources such as sunlight, wind, and trees are replaced naturally in a short time. Using a resource sustainably means not using it faster than it is replaced, such as pumping no more groundwater than rain refills. Natural hazards include earthquakes, hurricanes, floods, and volcanic eruptions. Mitigation reduces their harm, for example with stronger building codes, raised homes, levees, dunes, and wetlands that absorb storm water. Strong earthquakes are much rarer than weak ones.

concepts.definition: Evaporation → condensation → precipitation → runoff and infiltration.
concepts.tip: Evaporation goes up; precipitation comes down.

concepts.definition: Photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the air. Respiration, burning fuels, and volcanoes add it.
concepts.tip: Growing plants take carbon in; burning lets it out.

concepts.definition: Soil bacteria change nitrogen gas into forms plants can absorb; decomposers return nitrogen to the soil.
concepts.tip: Plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly.

concepts.definition: Coal, oil, and natural gas formed from ancient buried organisms over millions of years.
concepts.tip: Fossil = from ancient life.

concepts.definition: Renewable: replaced naturally in a short time. Nonrenewable: limited, takes millions of years to form.
concepts.tip: Sun, wind, water, trees: renewable. Coal, oil, gas: not.

concepts.definition: Actions that reduce the damage from a natural hazard, such as raising homes or keeping dunes and wetlands.
concepts.tip: Mitigate = make the harm smaller.

points: Sustainable use: do not use a resource faster than it is replaced.
Time to reach a level = distance left ÷ rate.
Averages from past data do not guarantee exact future events.

summary: This chapter covers Earth's major parts, the atmosphere, the oceans, and the solid Earth, and how they interact. Many questions ask you to read a table of measurements or explain a cause and effect.

The atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen. From the ground up, its layers are the troposphere (where weather happens), the stratosphere (which contains the ozone layer that absorbs much of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation), the mesosphere, and the thermosphere. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapor trap heat near the surface; adding more of them warms the climate. Wind blows from high air pressure toward low air pressure.
The oceans hold salt water and move heat around the planet. Warm currents such as the Gulf Stream make nearby coasts milder. When water stays too warm, corals can bleach.

Inside Earth are the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core. The crust is broken into tectonic plates, and most earthquakes and volcanoes happen near plate boundaries. Where plates move apart at mid-ocean ridges, new ocean crust forms. Weathering by wind, water, and ice breaks rock down over time.

concepts.definition: Crust (where we live), mantle, liquid outer core, solid inner core.
concepts.tip: Crust is thin, like the skin of an apple.

concepts.definition: About 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen. Layers: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere.
concepts.tip: Weather happens in the troposphere.

concepts.definition: Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs much of the Sun's UV radiation.
concepts.tip: Ozone = UV shield.

concepts.definition: Gases such as CO₂ and water vapor trap heat given off by Earth's surface.
concepts.tip: Ozone is about UV; greenhouse gases are about trapped heat.

concepts.definition: Earth's crust is broken into moving plates. Most earthquakes and volcanoes happen at plate boundaries.
concepts.tip: Look at plate edges for earthquakes and volcanoes.

concepts.definition: Physical weathering breaks rock without changing its minerals; chemical weathering changes the minerals.
concepts.tip: Chemical weathering makes a new material; physical does not.

points: Ozone layer (UV protection) and the greenhouse effect (trapped heat) are different things.
Average rate of change = change ÷ number of years.
Plates moving apart make new crust; plates moving together can make trenches or mountains.

summary: This chapter covers Earth's place in space and how scientists know Earth's age. Questions often give a short table of planet data or describe rock layers.

The Sun is a star, one of billions in the Milky Way galaxy. A star like the Sun becomes a red giant near the end of its life and then a white dwarf; only much more massive stars can become neutron stars or black holes. Earth spins on its axis about once every 24 hours, which causes day and night, and orbits the Sun once a year. The tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons.
The Moon's gravity is the main cause of tides. In a solar eclipse the Moon is between the Sun and Earth; in a lunar eclipse Earth is in the middle.

Planets farther from the Sun take longer to orbit it. Earth's history is read from rocks. In undisturbed layers of sedimentary rock, the bottom layer is oldest, and fossils show what lived at different times. Radiometric dating uses half-life: each half-life, half of a radioactive element's atoms change, so counting how much is left tells the age of a rock.

concepts.definition: Caused by Earth spinning on its axis, about once every 24 hours.
concepts.tip: Spin = a day; orbit = a year.

concepts.definition: Caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, not by its distance from the Sun.
concepts.tip: Tilt toward the Sun = summer.

concepts.definition: Caused mainly by the Moon's gravity pulling on the oceans.
concepts.tip: The Moon is the main cause; the Sun adds a smaller pull.

concepts.definition: Solar: Moon between Sun and Earth. Lunar: Earth between Sun and Moon.
concepts.tip: Solar = Sun is blocked; lunar = Moon is darkened.

concepts.definition: Main-sequence star → red giant → white dwarf.
concepts.tip: Only very massive stars become black holes.

concepts.definition: The time for half of a radioactive element's atoms to change. After 2 half-lives, one-fourth remains.
concepts.tip: Count how many times you halve, then multiply by the half-life.

points: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, so distance does not cause seasons.
Undisturbed rock layers: oldest at the bottom.
Use only the data given; do not add facts the table does not show.
